text.p: Copper ended lower on the London Metal Exchange after volatile trade that lead the LME to monitor trading, while gold also declined.

Copper dropped in late trade and premia for prompt delivery contracted sharply. Earlier, traders said it seemed that someone -- possibly a European merchant house -- had got got control of a chunk of warehouse stocks. Speculators were having to pay big premiums to cover short positions.

The LME has been particularly vigilant since last June when copper prices crashed on news that Sumitomo Corp of Japan made losses that have been put at $2.6 billion in what it alleged was rogue trading in copper.
Copper traded around support levels during the london afternoon at $2,200 a tonne, around $50 down on Tuesday.

Aluminium was depressed by negative charts after a recent double failure at $1,640, and dropped under liquidation to near $1,600 at one point. Last business was at $1,613, down $19, with the market needing to regain $1,625 to head off further losses.

Lead dived to the lowest levels since October 1995 during the kerb, as bearish sentiment from copper cascaded through the market. Last business was at $669 a tonne, down $6 from Tuesday, but above a $662 low. Technicians see the market ranging down to $640/650.
Zinc slithered down to a low-point of $1,120 at one stage, although the selling pressure was not so intense. Last trade was at $1,126, down $4 from yesterday.
Nickel trading was erratic, although the market was well defended on dips towards $7,150. However, the overall direction was downwards, and last trade was at $7,180, down $40.

Tin retreated to the $5,800 level, but was supported here, albeit in fairly low-key trading. Final business was at this level, down $75 from Tuesday, with more losses likely as physical interest is said to be running at a low ebb.
In precious metals gold traded sharply lower to end in London $2.00 from Tuesday at $351.05 an ounce, under pressure from a firmer dollar.

New York precious metals futures also ended lower, on good volumes, and have now given back about half of the sharp bounce seen last week. COMEX April gold, now the active contract, ended down $2.50 an ounce at $353.20, but off the session lows at $352.70. Estimated total volume was 68,000 contracts.

Spot gold ended quoted $351.00/50 an ounce, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $351.10 and the New York close Tuesday at $352.90/40. Spot gold saw a three year low around $347.00 in mid-January.

London March futures for the world benchmark Brent Blend of crude oil were firmer by almost 50 cents a barrel on what traders said were forecasts for cold weather in the United States, that may boost demand for heating oil, and on news of political instability in Iraq.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry, said the White House sees internal "struggles for power" in Iraq. McCurry was commenting on reports by a senior U.S. military official that President Saddam Hussein has put his wife under house arrest.
NYMEX oil prices also rallied sharply after bullish weather forecasts and the political tensions in Iraq triggered heavy short covering in crude and heating oil.
After trading in tight range since Monday, Feb heat settled up 2.01 cents at 68.84 cents a gallon while March crude ended up 57 cents at $24.47 a barrel.
CBOT wheat futures closed lower as the market floundered while awaiting direction from the export sector, traders said.

The market was stirred early this week by talk India and Egypt were entering the market for optional-origin wheat. But the market was skeptical the U.S. will land much, if any of the business. Wheat closed 2-3/4 cents per bushel lower to 1/2 higher, with March down 2-3/4 at $3.70-1/4.
